Halpin was born June 14, 1906, and grew up in New Haven, Connecticut. He was apparently the first student from New Haven to attend Notre Dame. He found several jobs to help defray tuition and living expenses. He was fascinated by accounts about Knute Rockne and the Notre Dame football team. He worked his way up the athletic manager system until named senior manager. He was Rockne's last manager, also serving as Rockne's secretary and business manager.
335: Endnotes continue. Halpin's leadership extended beyond sports. He realized the campus needed a laundry service, so he started one, creating the logo 'La UND ry.' The business was so profitable the University eventually took it over. After the tragic Rockne plane crash in March 1931, Halpin was deputized by the university president to fly to Kansas and escort Rockne's remains back to Notre Dame. Upon graduation in June 1931, he was hired by MGM to serve as the 'Rockne expert' for the film 'Knute Rockne of Notre Dame.' After that, he returned to the East coast with his new bride, Margaret Hyland Halpin, renting an apartment at 425 Riverside Drive in Manhattan at the height of the Depression. His first job was selling hearing aids on 42nd Street. He was so skilled a salesman that he out-sold the major brand 'Dictograph,' which advertised heavily on the radio. Dictograph hired him away and made him a sales manager, then vice president. His first child was born in 1932, and the family was financially well off. Halpin's son, Dan Halpin, Jr., recalls that his father mentioned Napoleon Hill frequently, and was the best man at Blair Hill's wedding. The elder Halpin was instrumental in providing Blair with a hearing aid. Dan Halpin always spoke highly of Napoleon Hill and was proud of his inclusion in Think and Grow Rich!
336: Endnotes continue. The Halpins stayed in Manhattan until 1940. His next move was to Haddonfield, New Jersey, where he was hired as vice president and general manager of sales at the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) in Camden, N.J. His new role was to market and merchandise a new entertainment system called television. He spent the next 12 years with RCA. In 1952, the family moved to Montclair, N.J., where he became vice president and general manager of DuMont Television. He ended his career as an account executive with Young & Rubicam Advertising, specializing in the General Electric television account. While his career had many firsts, he was duly proud of being the first sales executive to convince a major hotel chain to put a television in each of its rooms, in the early 1950s. He was the creative genius who convinced owners of television sets that life would be better if they owned two televisions—the second being known as a 'mother-in-law' TV. As a result, RCA sold millions of sets. He was also known as the primary force behind the sales strategy for the introduction and merchandising of color television. He was truly a pioneer in the early days of the television industry. Halpin died in his sleep at age 63 on August 21, 1970, about six weeks before Napoleon Hill passed away.
